mech: One big threat from the northern steppe rewarded a single centralised state that could mass troops on one frontier; divided regimes in the north were picked off.
Mirror-empire dynamics: steppe confederations and Chinese empires grew in step, each forcing the other to scale up; most mega-empires formed on the steppe edge.
Northern China sat next to the largest steppe in the world, so steppe-trained cavalry and frontier regimes kept re-creating a big northern state that conquered the south.
Steppe empires lived off tribute from a rich unified China, so they rose with it and fell with it; Manchurian frontier regimes, not Mongol ones, conquered China when it was divided.
A large, flat, fertile core with no mountain barriers lets whoever holds it snowball; in their simulations China unifies and Europe does not on geography alone.
Alps, Pyrenees, Carpathians and seas cut Europe into defensible cores, so no ruler could take them all.
Europe's indented coast, peninsulas and islands sheltered many small states, while China's smooth coast and two linked river basins favoured one.
Europe faced threats from many directions (Vikings, Magyars, Mongols, Ottomans) and none decisive, so local lords defended themselves and power stayed dispersed.
The steppe hammer that reunified China in 1279 never fell on western Europe: the Mongols turned back in 1242 and Europe kept its many states.
note: A deliberately weak link: it marks the counterfactual rather than a mechanism; most historians doubt the Mongols could have held the forested west.

mech: Qin and Han made 'Great Unity' (da yitong) the only legitimate order: every regional ruler after a collapse claimed the whole, so division was always an interregnum.
A shared Confucian agrarian-empire model gave elites a script for rebuilding one bureaucratic state rather than many.
The examinations tied the ambitions of local elites to service in one empire-wide state, giving them a stake in reunification instead of regional independence.

An early bureaucracy let Chinese rulers tax and govern without bargaining with local assemblies, so a conqueror could rebuild the empire from the top down; Europe's rulers, lacking one, had to share power with many local bodies.

Qin won by 'self-strengthening' reforms (mass conscription, direct taxation) that beat the balance of power; once won, the model of the universal state was available to every later unifier, unlike Europe where balancing kept working.
With the great clans gone, Song elites were scattered local lineages: too fragmented to resist the throne, which made the empire durable but weak at taxing.
Constant wars among European peers built strong fiscal-military states but kept the system multipolar; China fought mostly frontier wars with nomads, which favoured one centre.
Many similar-sized rivals with cheap access to gunpowder technology fought often, which made military innovation pay.
Dissident thinkers could move to a rival court or printer; no single authority could suppress heterodoxy, so ideas competed on merit.
The Republic of Letters rewarded verifiable new knowledge with reputation across borders.
Europe's escape from a Roman-style empire was the necessary, not sufficient, condition: competition among states, churches, cities and merchants made the British breakthrough possible.
Gunpowder learning gave Europeans the military edge to seize trade, colonies and the Atlantic's resources.

A unified empire with no peer rivals needed little revenue, so it could tax lightly and keep capital in the countryside; Europe's warring states taxed heavily and huddled industry inside city walls, which later favoured capital-intensive production.
A hegemonic empire with no maritime rivals could afford to shut the coast; no European prince could have banned his merchants and kept up with neighbours.
Offensive war on every frontier required permanent professional armies under commanders who held civil and fiscal power in their regions.

view: Po Chu-i (Bai Juyi), as read by Waley
mech: Disastrous levies for the Yunnan campaigns of 751-754, under Yang Guozhong, cost the court the loyalty of the capital region.
An Lushan commanded three frontier armies, about 180,000 men, while the capital had no comparable force.
After Li Linfu died in 752, the new chief minister Yang Guozhong set out to destroy An Lushan; rebellion was the general's pre-emptive answer.
War destroyed the registration machinery and drove millions off the rolls; the 36-million fall is mostly lost paperwork plus refugees, not deaths.

view: Arthur Waley (1918) and the popular death-toll tradition
mech: Reading the registers literally, the war 'cost thirty million men', which would make it one of history's deadliest wars.
note: Kept as the rejected reading so the map can show both: few historians now accept a literal death toll of this size.

mech: With the head-tax base gone, the court turned to an indirect tax that no rebel governor could hide: salt.
The equal-field system assumed accurate registers of every household; once they were gone, a tax on actual property was the only way to tax.
To end the war the court pardoned rebel generals and left them their armies in Hebei.
Refugees fled the ravaged north for the Yangzi and the south, and stayed; the state came to depend on southern grain shipped up the Grand Canal.
High monopoly prices created a huge smuggling trade; Huang Chao and Wang Xianzhi were salt smugglers whose networks became armies.
Weak monsoons meant droughts and harvest failures in the 870s, swelling the bandit armies.
Cave and lake records line up dry phases with the ends of the Tang, Yuan and Ming, suggesting a climate trigger for dynastic collapse.
note: Critics note the dating uncertainties and that the late Tang was already fragmented by 880.

mech: Epitaphs show the great clans lived concentrated in the two capitals; Huang Chao's sack of Chang'an in 881 and later massacres in 904-905 killed them off as a class.
The rebels' destruction of the capital left the court a puppet of the warlord Zhu Wen, who deposed the last emperor in 907.
A century of semi-independent provinces left the dynasty with a shrunken tax base and no monopoly of force.
Huang Chao's army took Guangzhou and, by Arab accounts, massacred its foreign merchant community.
A severe drought lasting nearly seven decades did not make the Uyghur empire collapse, wage war or break up; the khaganate fell to the Kyrgyz in 840 for political reasons.
note: Kept at very low confidence on purpose: the paper argues against this causal step.

mech: The centre of population moved to the wet-rice south, whose rivers and canals made cheap water transport and dense markets possible.
Early-ripening rice allowed double cropping and planting on higher, drier land, raising grain output per acre.
Once the state stopped allotting land and taxed property in cash, land and labour markets opened; the Song inherited a commercialised countryside.
With the old clans gone, the Song recruited officials by open examination; tens of thousands sat each round by the 1100s.
Mass examination candidacy created a market for printed classics and commentaries.
Demand from a huge army, a capital of a million people and a monetised economy pushed iron output up roughly sixfold between 806 and 1078.
Charcoal grew scarce on the deforested north China plain, so Kaifeng and the Hebei smelters switched to coal and coke.
Sichuan's heavy iron coins were so bulky that merchants issued deposit certificates; the state took over the scheme in 1024.
Endless war against the Xi Xia and payments to the Liao drove Wang Anshi to squeeze revenue from commerce.
The tea-and-horse monopoly bought war horses by crushing a thriving private tea industry in Sichuan: the state could also kill growth.
note: A negative contribution: the monopoly weakened, not strengthened, the commercial economy it fed on.

mech: Growth was driven by the fiscal state: military procurement and cash taxes monetised the economy, and output fell when the state stopped buying.
Loss of Kaifeng and the north to the Jurchen in 1127 cut off the iron industry's main market; Hartwell's northern output collapsed.
note: The link reads as harm: the conquest ended the boom.

mech: The Jin captured two emperors at Kaifeng; the court refounded itself in the south.
The Wujing Zongyao of 1044 records gunpowder formulae: Song state arsenals turned an alchemical discovery into a weapon.
The Song set the level China would hover around for seven centuries: about 1,225 (2011 dollars) in 1000 and 1,222 in 1090, against 1,151 for Britain in 1000.
The Naito hypothesis: the end of aristocratic rule between Tang and Song began China's 'early modern' age of autocracy, commoners and markets.
Talent went into memorising the classics for the examinations instead of mathematics and controlled experiment, so invention stayed experience-based and grew only with population.
'Bureaucratic feudalism' fostered applied science for the state but never let a merchant class gain the autonomy that, in Europe, joined craft to mathematics.
Cheap labour and an efficient traditional technology left almost no gap between what was and what could be made, so labour-saving invention did not pay.
With one empire and one orthodoxy, an innovator had nowhere else to go; there was no Chinese Republic of Letters spanning rival states.
China lacked autonomous corporate bodies (universities, chartered towns) with legal room for disinterested inquiry; Neo-Confucian orthodoxy set the curriculum.
From 1313 Zhu Xi's commentaries were the official examination curriculum, until 1905.
An 'industrial Enlightenment' joined scientific method to craft, making invention systematic.
Without a scientific culture of its own, China could not generate the stream of industrial technique that drove Europe ahead.
Severe drought in the 1180s fed tribal war and broke old hierarchies, the instability in which Temujin's new order arose.
Temujin broke up the old tribes and rebuilt them into decimal units loyal to him, promoting by merit and loyalty, not lineage.
A supratribal steppe polity could only be held together by war and the redistribution of plunder from sedentary neighbours.
Fifteen unusually wet, warm years raised grassland productivity, and with it the herds of horses and livestock that carried armies and political power.
Drought pushed hungry nomads outward onto settled lands.
note: Kept as the rival reading that Pederson et al. reverse: the conquests coincide with the wet phase, not the dry one.

mech: The Mongol campaigns against the Jin culminated in the fall and sack of Zhongdu (Beijing).
Twenty-three years of war ended the Jurchen Jin state in 1234.
Massacre, flight, famine and disease: registered households in the north fell from about 8 million under the Jin to about 1 million in the first Mongol count.
After the five-year siege of Xiangyang, Bayan's army took the Song capital Hangzhou without a sack.
A steppe empire, not a Chinese one, ended three centuries of division between Liao, Xi Xia, Jin and Song.
Chinggisid rulers moved artisans, doctors, astronomers and goods deliberately across their realm.
Ancient DNA places the ancestor of the Black Death strain near Lake Issyk-Kul around 1338; caravans and armies across the Mongol world carried it west to the Black Sea by 1346.
Batu and Subutai's western campaign destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohi in April 1241.
A wet spring flooded the Hungarian plain, ruined pasture and mobility and brought famine, pushing the Mongols to pull back.
News of the Great Khan's death made princes like Batu weigh the succession, the classic explanation in Juvaini and later writers.
Across two millennia, a one-standard-deviation fall in rainfall raised the chance of nomadic attack on China; drought hit pasture harder than farmland.
Cold phases cut farm output, food prices rose and wars, famines and population falls followed in cycles across the preindustrial world.
Jia Lu's dyke works massed 150,000 conscripted labourers on the flooded plain, where the White Lotus rising began in 1351.
Printing chao to pay for the dykes and the war wrecked the currency and the trust of the propertied.
The huge dyke project was financed largely by new issues of paper money.
Zhu Yuanzhang rose from a Red Turban band to defeat rival warlords, proclaim the Ming at Nanjing and drive the Yuan court north.
The rebellions stripped the Yuan of China south of the Wall; the court fled to Mongolia in 1368.
The conquest ended the north's industrial base and the Song-Yuan-Ming transition shifted growth to the Yangzi delta, at a lower level of technology than Kaifeng's.
The ban drove trade into smuggling and the 'wokou' piracy of the 1550s, until Fujian officials argued that licensing trade was cheaper than war.
Under early Ming autarky and the command economy, GDP per head slid from about 1,400 (2011 dollars) in 1400 to about 1,200 by 1500.
After Yuan and early Ming paper money became worthless, Chinese households and merchants turned to silver bullion, and the state followed.
China's silver price was roughly double Europe's and Japan's: an arbitrage gap that pulled the world's silver east.
Chinese silver demand made the Acapulco-Manila route pay; Manila, founded 1571, became where Potosí silver met Chinese silk.
Potosí, with mercury amalgamation from 1572, supplied the silver that the galleons carried to Manila.
Licensed Fujian junks from Yuegang were the Chinese side of the Manila trade.
Abundant imported silver made it possible to commute taxes and labour service to silver across the empire.
American silver via Manila joined Japanese silver in the 1570s, just as the Single Whip tied the treasury to it.
Piecemeal local commutation of taxes to silver over a century was consolidated into one payment.
Expelling the Portuguese removed the Macau carriers of Japanese silver to China.
Falling silver supply raised its value against copper and grain, so taxes fixed in silver became heavier just as harvests failed; hoarding and defaults followed.
Silver imports in the 1640s were near their peak levels and silver prices did not rise as the crisis theory needs; the monetary crisis is mostly a myth.
note: The low confidence encodes von Glahn's rejection of the Atwell link, not weak evidence for his own view.

mech: Eruptions in 1640-41 (Komaga-take in Japan, Parker in the Philippines) loaded the stratosphere with sulphate in East Asia's coldest years.
The Little Ice Age's deepest phase reached China in the 1620s-1640s, shortening growing seasons in the north.
A weakened monsoon in the cold years brought the worst run of drought in north China in five centuries.
Harvest failures in Shaanxi and Henan turned bandit bands into mass armies of the hungry.
Famine, refugees and locusts set the stage for epidemic disease across the north China plain.
Disease emptied Beijing's garrison in 1643-44, and the walls fell to Li Zicheng with little fight.
Surtaxes for the Manchu front fell on the starving north, and unpaid soldiers deserted to the rebels.
The Ming fiscal system had low, fixed quotas and no way to borrow; a new war could only be paid with ad hoc surtaxes.
Li Zicheng, a laid-off courier from the 1629 cuts to the postal relay system, built the largest rebel army.
Li Zicheng's army took Beijing on 25 April 1644 and the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself.
General Wu Sangui let the Manchu banners through Shanhaiguan to drive Li Zicheng from Beijing; the Qing stayed.
Once again a frontier conquest regime rebuilt one empire, and then doubled its territory into Inner Asia.
The fall of the Ming and the conquest wars were the single largest episode of the 17th-century global crisis, with China's population perhaps a fifth smaller by 1660.
The conquest war cut population, so output per head briefly rose as survivors farmed better land: 1,217 in 1600, about 1,330 by 1661 and 1,543 by 1700, before the Qing slide.
note: A Malthusian rebound: the war worked against the long decline for a few decades.

mech: A century of internal peace, new upland crops and frontier settlement let population nearly triple.
Maize and sweet potatoes from the Americas let migrants farm hills that would not take rice or wheat.
Chinese families limited births and the state damped famine; growth came less from a Malthusian rush than from controlled fertility and falling mortality.
More people per acre made labour cheaper and land, fuel and draught animals dearer, deepening the trap.
'Involution': delta households absorbed more family labour into cotton spinning and silk for ever smaller returns per day, so output rose without development.
Output grew more slowly than population: GDP per head falls from about 1,543 (1700) to about 858 (1850) in their series.
Jiangnan and England were both near ecological limits around 1750; Jiangnan had no coal next door and no colonies, so it could not break out.
Coal freed Britain from the land: by 1800 its coal supplied heat equal to millions of acres of woodland.
Slave-grown American cotton, sugar and timber were 'ghost acres' that fed Britain's factories without using British land.
Plague killed a third or more of Europeans; labour became scarce and real wages doubled, and in the North Sea economies stayed high.
Dear labour and cheap coal made Britain the only place where the spinning jenny and the steam engine paid at first.

view: Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden
mech: Unskilled wages in Beijing, Canton and Suzhou bought roughly a bare-bones subsistence basket, like Milan or Delhi, while London's bought several times that.
Sustained per-capita growth in Britain, then north-western Europe, turned a modest gap into a chasm by 1900.
By 1400 Italy, Holland and Britain were all ahead of China in GDP per head, and the gap widened after 1700 as China's fell: the divergence began long before the industrial revolution.
A full national account for Huating-Lou in the 1820s puts the richest part of China at roughly half the Netherlands' GDP per head.
Secure peasant possession in Jiangnan let families subdivide land and add labour, while English landlords and tenants faced competitive markets that forced productivity gains.
Pre-modern 'efflorescences', Song China among them, always ended; Britain's was the first to become permanent, through coal-fuelled engineering.
Asia led the world economy until about 1800; Europe used American silver to buy into Asian trade and overtook it only when Asia entered a downturn.
In a huge empire the throne could not monitor its agents, so it kept taxes low to limit extortion; by 1850 revenue per head had fallen in real terms and the state was thin on the ground.
Britain taxed several times more per head than Qing China and spent it on a navy and infrastructure that protected trade; China's light state could not.
The Ming-Qing wage and price records underlying every comparison are too thin and local to fix the date of divergence with confidence.
note: A sceptical link: it keeps the decline-to-divergence step open rather than asserting it.

mech: Confining European trade to Canton channelled the East India Company's Bengal opium through a single port and its smugglers.
Silver flowed out to pay for opium and as world silver output fell after Latin American independence; copper-earning farmers paid silver taxes that doubled in real terms.
The break-up of the Spanish peso standard after 1810 disrupted the coin China trusted; Chinese merchants discounted new republican coins and exported silver, raising the opium-silver stakes.
Alarm at the silver drain drove the Daoguang emperor to send Lin Zexu to destroy the opium stocks in 1839, which Britain answered with war.
Defeat discredited the Qing in the south; trade shifted to Shanghai, and demobilised militia and unemployed porters filled the secret societies of Guangdong and Guangxi.
His collapse and visions came after the 1837 failure; the 1843 failure sent him back to the Christian tract that explained them.
The God Worshippers, Hakka miners and charcoal burners in Guangxi, followed Hong as the Heavenly King against the Manchu demons.
A tripled population on a nearly fixed land area left the poor south with surplus young men, land feuds between Hakka and Punti, and no frontier left.
Against the White Lotus the Qing first relied on gentry-led local militia (tuanlian), the template Zeng Guofan scaled up.
With the banner and Green Standard armies beaten, the court let Zeng Guofan raise a private army of Hunanese.
Zeng Guoquan's Xiang Army besieged and stormed Nanjing in July 1864.
Britain dropped its neutrality to protect the Shanghai trade; British guns and steamers held Shanghai in 1862 and kept the delta's customs revenue flowing to the Qing.
Sieges, massacres, famine and disease emptied the richest region of China; survivors wrote of corpses unburied for years.
The Taiping marched down the Yangzi and took Nanjing in March 1853, making it their Heavenly Capital.
Victory left provincial armies and their lijin revenues in the hands of governors-general like Zeng and Li Hongzhang.
Victory over the Taiping gave the scholar-generals the authority to rebuild the Confucian order and buy Western arms.
When the provinces declared independence in 1911, the court had no army of its own to call on.
China's most advanced economy was gutted just as Britain's industrial lead compounded.
Tokugawa villages already had commercial farming, by-employment, literacy and rural industry; Meiji factories drew on this workforce and its skills.
An industrious revolution: families worked longer and harder in place of animals and capital, building the habits and markets industry needed.
Under the guns of the American squadron the shogunate signed the Kanagawa treaty (1854), then the Harris treaty (1858) opening ports to trade.
Moving from near-autarky to free trade, Japan exported what it was relatively good at (silk, tea) and imported cloth and metal; static gains were around 8-9 percent of GDP.
World prices rushed in: silk and tea prices jumped, rice and living costs soared and gold drained out at the old gold-silver ratio, feeding anti-foreign anger.
Signing unequal treaties without imperial sanction made the shogun look like the foreigners' servant; activists rallied to "revere the emperor, expel the barbarian".
Satsuma and Choshu, having learned Western arms the hard way at Kagoshima (1863) and Shimonoseki (1864), allied in 1866 and overthrew the shogunate.
The Boshin war ended with the surrender of the last Tokugawa holdouts at Hakodate in 1869.
Abolishing the domains (1871) let the new state replace 270 domain rice levies with one national money tax.
A fixed money tax on a rising farm output transferred agricultural surplus to the state and to investors in the early decades.
The Charter Oath's promise to seek knowledge throughout the world became a national school system within four years.
Literate, numerate workers and engineers trained at home made imported technology work.
The new government borrowed in London to build the Tokyo-Yokohama line and later nationalised the trunk lines.
Districts reached by rail saw more firm formation and larger firms, as markets widened.
A backward economy industrialises in a spurt led by the state and big banks, adopting the newest large-scale technology at once.
Japan's state and local associations standardised silkworm eggs and reeling, and silk earnings paid for imported machines; China's fragmented state could not do the same.
A conscript army and a modern navy, supplied by new arsenals and shipyards, defeated the Qing fleet and armies in 1894-95.
China fought with Li Hongzhang's regional Beiyang fleet and army while other provinces stood aside.
Self-strengthening grafted arsenals onto a Confucian order that blocked deeper reform; defeat by Japan in 1895 exposed the limit.
Japanese GDP per head grew slowly but steadily from the early 1700s while China's fell; by 1850 Japan was ahead (about 1,436 against 858 in 2011 dollars) though far behind Britain.
With foreign trade restricted and silver exports banned, Japan substituted domestic silk, cotton and sugar for imports, building rural industry.
The Black Death of 1346-53 was the first and deadliest wave of the second pandemic.
